title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 60
paragraphs: At that moment he answered the Corinthian mildly; and to Eurybiades he now said none of the things he had said before — about how, if they set sail from Salamis, the fleet would scatter in different directions — for it was unseemly to make accusations against the allies in their presence. Instead he held to another line of argument, saying: “Now it is in your power to save Greece, if you will follow my advice, which is to stay here and fight a sea-battle, and not follow the counsel of those among these men who urge you to move the ships to the Isthmus. Hear both options and compare them. If you engage battle at the Isthmus, you will fight in an open sea — into which it is in no way convenient for us to go, since our ships are heavier and fewer in number than the enemy's. Secondly, you will hand over Salamis, Megara, and Aegina to destruction, even if we succeed in everything else; for with their fleet will come their land-army too, and so you yourself will lead them to the Peloponnese and will put the safety of all Greece at risk. If, however, you do as I say, you will find in it all the advantages I shall describe: first, by engaging in a narrow space with few ships against many, if the fighting turns out as it is reasonable to expect, we shall have a great advantage — for fighting a sea-battle in a narrow space is to our advantage, while fighting in a wide open space is to theirs. Next, Salamis will be preserved, where our children and wives have been taken for safety; and there is this further point, which you value most of all: by remaining here you will fight in defense of the Peloponnese just as much as if the battle were at the Isthmus, and you will not lead the enemy to the Peloponnese, if you are wise. Then, if what I expect comes to pass and we win a victory with our ships, the barbarians will not come against you at the Isthmus nor advance beyond Attica, but will retreat in disorder; and we shall gain by the preservation of Megara, Aegina, and Salamis — the place where an oracle also tells us we shall overcome our enemies. When men take reasonable counsel for themselves, reasonable outcomes tend to follow; but if they do not take reasonable counsel, God is not usually inclined to attach himself to human judgment.”
